USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the current posture and keep negotiating under the May 19 framework — preserve the Section 301 tariff list and ZTE ban as leverage while pressing China to convert its vague purchase pledge into concrete commitments and genuine IP/tech-transfer reform. Do not launch new escalatory action, which would collapse the fragile ceasefire and trigger China's $50B retaliation against US agriculture, autos, and aircraft; do not fully concede before structural protections are locked in. Send a follow-up team to Beijing to nail down dollar figures and enforcement details, keeping the tariff threat explicitly on the table as the guarantee.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to the US is moderate but real, so I place it at +0.3. No tariff has yet been imposed — the $50B Section 301 list is still in public comment/hearing phase with a final list not expected until June/July, and the US economy (industrial production up, consumer sentiment ~98, firm dollar, Fed funds 1.70%) shows no sign yet of being harmed. At the same time, China has already conceded by agreeing to significantly increase purchases (May 19 joint statement; Mnuchin: trade war 'on hold'), which is leverage the US should bank. The residual threat is that the deal is vague — no dollar amounts, no structural IP/tech-transfer reform, ZTE unresolved — and if talks collapse, China's ~$50B retaliatory list (soybeans, autos, aircraft) hits the farm belt and aerospace/ICT supply chains. That justifies a cautious, non-provocative action stance at 0.0 (negotiate): escalation now would forfeit the purchase concession already won and invite symmetric retaliation, while full concession would give away the Section 301 and ZTE leverage before structural protections are secured. Holding the credible threat as negotiation leverage while pushing for concrete, enforceable commitments is the balance that preserves leverage and minimizes escalation risk.
key_factors: Section 301 ~$50B tariff list not yet implemented; still in public comment/hearing phase through late May, with final list not expected until June/July
May 19 joint statement: China agreed to 'significantly increase' US purchases; Mnuchin declared trade war 'on hold' — a Chinese concession and de-escalation
US macro strong and insulated so far: industrial production rising, consumer sentiment ~98, dollar firm (~111.7 broad index), Fed funds 1.70% (normal tightening)
China's ~$50B retaliatory list (soybeans, autos, aircraft) exposes US farm belt and exporters to retaliation if talks collapse
No structural IP/tech-transfer reform secured yet — only vague purchase pledges, no dollar amounts, ZTE unresolved

sources_cited.excerpt: US and China release joint statement after talks: China agrees to 'significantly increase' purchases of US goods and services. Mnuchin says trade war is 'on hold.' Markets rally.
US Commerce Department bans ZTE from buying US components (denial order). Major non-tariff escalation.
US industrial production rising through April (103.33), consumer sentiment 98, broad dollar index ~111.7.
Joint statement vague — no dollar amounts; did not indicate whether US will back down from tariff plans; ZTE not mentioned; Schumer criticizes lack of concrete IP protections.
Section 301 comment period ended May 11, hearing May 15 (post-hearing rebuttals due May 22); final list unlikely before mid-June/July.
